questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient changes behavior after a group discussion; what broad process is this?
questions.explanation: Social influence is the process by which others' behavior or presence changes an individual's thoughts, feelings, or actions. The group discussion fits this broadly.
questions.hint: Behavior change due to others is social influence.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician reads that a patient witnessed an emergency but did not help because others were present.

questions.stem: What phenomenon explains the patient's inaction?
questions.explanation: The presence of others reduces the likelihood of helping in an emergency. This is the bystander effect, driven partly by diffusion of responsibility.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician sees a patient rate members of their own group more positively than outsiders.

questions.stem: What bias is shown?
questions.explanation: Preferential evaluation of one's own group is ingroup favoritism. It can occur even with arbitrary group distinctions.
questions.hint: Preferring one's own group is ingroup favoritism.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether people blame victims for misfortune; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Present participants with a victim scenario and measure blame attributions, comparing conditions that emphasize random versus deserved outcomes.

questions.explanation: Manipulating whether outcomes seem deserved tests just-world beliefs. Blaming victims more when outcomes seem deserved supports the concept.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient first agrees to a small request, then a larger one; explain the technique.

answer.exemplar: This is foot-in-the-door: initial compliance with a small request increases later compliance with a larger related request through self-perception.

questions.explanation: Small initial requests create a commitment that makes larger follow-ups more likely. This is foot-in-the-door, distinct from door-in-the-face.
questions.hint: Small request first, then larger one.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician observes a patient grows to like a song after hearing it repeatedly; what effect is this?
questions.explanation: Repeated exposure increases liking even without reinforcement. This is the mere exposure effect, distinct from conditioning or habituation.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify conformity in a group setting

stimulus.body: Clinician reads that a patient agrees with a group's wrong answer to avoid standing out.

questions.stem: What social process is shown?

options.misconception: labels public agreement as compliance technique

questions.explanation: Aligning one's answer with a group despite knowing it is wrong is conformity. Obedience requires an authority figure's directive.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a team that suppresses dissent to maintain harmony and makes a poor decision.

questions.stem: What group process is illustrated?

options.misconception: confuses decision failure with effort reduction
labels group harmony as loss of self

questions.explanation: Suppressing dissent to preserve harmony and producing a flawed decision is groupthink. Polarization shifts opinions to extremes instead.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether people overattribute behavior to personality; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Vary situational constraints in a scenario and measure how much participants attribute an actor's behavior to disposition versus situation.

questions.explanation: Manipulating situational constraints while measuring dispositional attribution tests the fundamental attribution error. Strong disposition attribution despite constraints supports FAE.
questions.hint: Vary situation and measure disposition attribution.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify a framing effect in a medical decision
questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient chooses surgery when survival rates are emphasized but not when mortality rates are; explain.

answer.exemplar: Equivalent information framed as gains versus losses shifts preferences, demonstrating a framing effect where logically identical options are evaluated differently.

questions.explanation: Gain-framed and loss-framed presentations of identical data produce different choices. This is the framing effect.
questions.hint: Equivalent info framed differently shifts choice.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician reads that no one in a group speaks up because each assumes others are comfortable; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses silent assumption with harmony pressure

questions.explanation: When individuals privately reject a norm but assume others accept it, pluralistic ignorance results. No one speaks because each misreads the group.
questions.hint: Private rejection with assumed group acceptance is pluralistic ignorance.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician notes a patient overestimates plane crash risk after seeing news coverage.

questions.stem: What heuristic explains this overestimation?

options.misconception: confuses ease of recall with prototype matching
labels recall ease as selective search

questions.explanation: Overestimating likelihood based on easily recalled examples is the availability heuristic. Recent news increases availability.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams an attitude with cognitive, affective, and behavioral components.

questions.stem: What is the three-part model of attitudes called?
questions.explanation: The ABC model captures affective, behavioral, and cognitive components of attitudes. It is a standard three-part framework.
questions.hint: Affective, behavioral, cognitive is the ABC model.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether people change attitudes after acting inconsistently; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Have participants perform a counterattitudinal behavior with low justification, then measure attitude change compared with high-justification controls.

questions.explanation: Low justification for counterattitudinal behavior maximizes dissonance and attitude change. High justification reduces dissonance.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician asks how prejudice differs from a stereotype; explain.

answer.exemplar: A stereotype is a cognitive belief about a group, while prejudice is a negative affective attitude toward a group; one is thought, the other feeling.

questions.explanation: Stereotypes are beliefs; prejudice is an attitude or feeling. They often co-occur but are conceptually distinct.
questions.hint: Stereotype is belief; prejudice is attitude.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient carefully weighs evidence before changing an attitude; which route is used?

options.misconception: confuses careful processing with cue reliance

questions.explanation: Careful evaluation of evidence reflects central route persuasion. The peripheral route relies on superficial cues instead.
questions.hint: Careful evidence weighing is central route.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the misinformation effect in eyewitnesses

stimulus.body: Clinician reads that an eyewitness's memory changed after leading questions.

questions.stem: What effect is demonstrated?

options.misconception: confuses content change with origin loss

questions.explanation: Leading questions can alter eyewitness memory, which is the misinformation effect. Source amnesia would leave content intact.
questions.hint: Leading questions altering memory is misinformation.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a patient rated as intelligent because they are attractive.

questions.stem: What bias is shown?

options.misconception: confuses trait spillover with causal judgment

questions.explanation: One positive trait (attractiveness) spilling over to unrelated traits (intelligence) is the halo effect. The horn effect is its negative counterpart.
questions.hint: Positive trait spilling over is halo effect.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify obedience in a Milgram-style case
questions.stem: Clinician wants to test how far people obey harmful orders; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Use a controlled experiment with an authority figure instructing participants to administer shocks, measuring compliance rates while ensuring ethical safeguards and debriefing.

questions.explanation: A controlled obedience paradigm with ethical safeguards measures compliance with authority. Debriefing is essential given potential distress.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician asks how normative and informational social influence differ; explain.

answer.exemplar: Normative influence seeks social approval and acceptance, while informational influence seeks accurate information in ambiguous situations.

questions.explanation: Normative influence is about fitting in; informational influence is about being right. The motives and situations differ.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes help is less likely when many bystanders are present; what mechanism explains this?
questions.explanation: Each bystander feels less personally responsible when others are present, reducing helping. This is diffusion of responsibility.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician reads that arbitrary group assignments still produce ingroup favoritism.

questions.stem: What does this finding show?
questions.explanation: Even arbitrary distinctions produce ingroup favoritism, showing the effect requires minimal group basis. Real groups are not necessary.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a patient blaming a victim to preserve a belief in a fair world.

questions.stem: What belief drives this victim-blaming?

options.misconception: labels belief protection as selective search
confuses fairness belief with positive expectation

questions.explanation: Blaming victims preserves the belief that the world is fair. This is the just-world belief in action.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether a large request followed by a smaller one increases compliance; design the study.

answer.exemplar: Present participants with an unreasonably large request, then a smaller target request, and compare compliance with a control receiving only the smaller request.

questions.explanation: The large-then-small sequence is door-in-the-face. Comparing to a small-only control isolates the technique's effect.
questions.hint: Large request first, then smaller target.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician asks whether mere exposure always increases liking; explain.

answer.exemplar: Mere exposure increases liking only up to a point; excessive repetition can produce boredom or annoyance, reversing the effect.

questions.explanation: The mere exposure effect is not unlimited. Overexposure can reduce liking through boredom or reactance.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient publicly agrees but privately disagrees; what conformity is this?

options.misconception: confuses public agreement with belief change
labels the pattern as a technique

questions.explanation: Agreeing publicly while disagreeing privately is compliance without private acceptance. True private acceptance involves genuine belief change.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician sees a group's average opinion become more extreme after discussion.

questions.stem: What process is shown?

options.misconception: confuses opinion shift with effort reduction

questions.explanation: Discussion shifting the group's average opinion toward a more extreme position is group polarization. Groupthink suppresses dissent instead.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a patient attributing their own lateness to traffic but others' lateness to laziness.

questions.stem: What bias is shown?

options.misconception: confuses self-other difference with other-only bias
labels perspective difference as selective search

questions.explanation: Attributing one's own behavior to situations but others' to traits is actor-observer bias. It differs from FAE, which concerns others only.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether losses loom larger than gains; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Present equivalent choices framed as gains versus losses and compare risk preferences, predicting risk aversion for gains and risk seeking for losses.

questions.explanation: Comparing risk preferences across gain and loss frames tests loss aversion. The asymmetry reveals losses looming larger.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Explain pluralistic ignorance in a classroom
questions.stem: Clinician notes students do not ask questions because each thinks others understand; explain.

answer.exemplar: This is pluralistic ignorance: each student privately feels confused but assumes others are not, so no one asks and the confusion persists.

questions.explanation: Private confusion combined with assumed group comprehension produces pluralistic ignorance. Speaking up would correct the misperception.
questions.hint: Private confusion with assumed group clarity.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient judges a person as a librarian based on stereotypes rather than base rates; what heuristic?

options.misconception: labels stereotype use as selective search
confuses prototype matching with recall ease

questions.explanation: Judging by prototype match while ignoring base rates is the representativeness heuristic. It often leads to base-rate neglect.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician notes a patient's stated attitude does not match their behavior.

questions.stem: What does this mismatch illustrate?
questions.explanation: Attitudes predict behavior only modestly; situational factors and specificity matter. Mismatch is common.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams participants paid little to lie who later change their attitude.

questions.stem: Why does low payment produce attitude change?
questions.explanation: Low payment provides insufficient external justification, so participants reduce dissonance by changing their attitude. High payment justifies the lie externally.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether reminding a group of a negative stereotype impairs performance; design the study.

answer.exemplar: Randomly assign participants to a stereotype-salient or neutral condition before a test, then compare performance while controlling for baseline ability.

questions.explanation: Manipulating stereotype salience with random assignment and baseline control isolates stereotype threat's effect on performance.
questions.hint: Manipulate stereotype salience and measure performance.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient changes attitude based on a speaker's attractiveness rather than arguments; explain.

answer.exemplar: This is peripheral route persuasion, where superficial cues like attractiveness drive attitude change without deep processing of the message.

questions.explanation: Superficial cues driving attitude change reflect the peripheral route. It produces less durable change than central route processing.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician reads that stress during a crime reduces eyewitness accuracy; what is a key factor?

options.misconception: misplaces the effect to retrieval only

questions.explanation: High stress can impair encoding of details, reducing later accuracy. It is not a uniform benefit or no-effect.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the fundamental attribution error in social perception

stimulus.body: Clinician notes a colleague attributes a patient's lateness to laziness, ignoring traffic.

questions.stem: What bias is shown?

options.misconception: confuses other-only bias with self-other difference

questions.explanation: Overattributing another's behavior to disposition while ignoring situation is the fundamental attribution error. Actor-observer bias includes self-attribution.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician compares obedience rates when the authority is distant versus present.

questions.stem: What does lower obedience at a distance suggest?
questions.explanation: Closer authority increases obedience; distance reduces it. Proximity is a key situational factor in obedience.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether people conform more in ambiguous situations; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Vary task ambiguity while measuring conformity to a group answer, predicting greater conformity when the correct answer is unclear.

questions.explanation: Greater conformity under ambiguity supports informational influence. Clear tasks reduce reliance on others.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician asks how to increase bystander helping; explain one strategy.

answer.exemplar: Directly addressing a specific bystander by name or eye contact reduces diffusion of responsibility and increases the chance of help.

questions.explanation: Singling out an individual overcomes diffusion of responsibility. It converts a crowd into a personal obligation.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes patients see outgroup members as more similar to each other than ingroup members; what is this?
questions.explanation: Perceiving outgroup members as more similar to each other than ingroup members is outgroup homogeneity. It is a perceptual bias distinct from favoritism.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the downside of just-world belief

stimulus.body: Clinician sees a patient blame a disadvantaged group for their plight to maintain fairness beliefs.

questions.stem: What harm can just-world belief cause?
questions.explanation: Just-world belief can lead to victim-blaming and prejudice by attributing misfortune to personal failings. Empathy may decrease instead.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a seller who secures agreement at a low price then raises it.

questions.stem: What technique is shown?

options.misconception: confuses price change with request escalation
confuses price change with product change

questions.explanation: Securing commitment at a low price then raising it is lowballing. The initial commitment drives continued compliance.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether mere exposure increases liking via fluency; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Manipulate exposure frequency and measure both liking and processing fluency, testing whether fluency mediates the exposure-liking link.

questions.explanation: If fluency mediates the exposure-liking relationship, the mere exposure effect operates partly through processing ease. Mediation analysis tests this.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician asks why people conform in Asch's line study; explain.

answer.exemplar: Participants conformed to avoid social rejection and because the unanimous group created doubt, even when the correct answer was obvious.

questions.explanation: Both normative pressure and informational doubt drove conformity. Unanimity was a strong condition for influence.
questions.hint: Rejection avoidance and doubt drove conformity.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to reduce groupthink in a treatment team; which strategy helps?
questions.explanation: Devil's advocacy introduces dissent and breaks premature consensus. Cohesion without dissent mechanisms worsens groupthink.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician notes a patient attributes successes to ability but failures to bad luck.

questions.stem: What bias is shown?
questions.explanation: Attributing successes internally and failures externally protects self-esteem. This is self-serving bias.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a patient choosing a treatment when framed as 90% survival versus 10% mortality.

questions.stem: Why do equivalent frames yield different choices?
questions.explanation: Loss aversion makes mortality frames more aversive, shifting choices. The facts are identical; only framing differs.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Explain how to correct pluralistic ignorance
questions.stem: Clinician wants to correct pluralistic ignorance in a group; design an intervention.

answer.exemplar: Provide anonymous feedback revealing others' private views, showing that the assumed norm is not actually held by most members.

questions.explanation: Revealing private views breaks the false consensus. Anonymous feedback reduces the pressure to conform publicly.
questions.hint: Reveal private views to break false consensus.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient's estimate stays close to an initial arbitrary number; explain.

answer.exemplar: This is anchoring: initial values serve as reference points, and adjustments from them are typically insufficient, biasing final estimates.

questions.explanation: Insufficient adjustment from an initial anchor biases judgments. The anchor can be arbitrary yet still influential.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician notes a patient changes attitude after acting inconsistently; what reduces the discomfort?
questions.explanation: Changing attitude to align with behavior reduces cognitive dissonance. People seek consistency among beliefs and actions.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician notes a patient rates a chosen option more favorably after deciding.

questions.stem: What phenomenon is shown?

options.misconception: misplaces the effect to before deciding

questions.explanation: Enhancing the chosen option's attractiveness after deciding reduces post-decision dissonance. It is a common reevaluation pattern.
questions.hint: Boosting the chosen option after deciding.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a patient performing better after being reminded of a positive group stereotype.

questions.stem: What effect is shown?

options.misconception: confuses positive with negative stereotype effects
confuses group stereotype with individual trait

questions.explanation: Performance improvement after a positive stereotype reminder is stereotype lift. It is the counterpart to stereotype threat.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether a message from an untrustworthy source becomes more persuasive over time; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Measure persuasion immediately and after a delay, comparing messages from low- versus high-credibility sources, to detect the sleeper effect.

questions.explanation: The sleeper effect occurs when source credibility is forgotten but message content remains, increasing persuasion over time. Delayed measurement detects it.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician asks why eyewitnesses often fail to identify a perpetrator holding a weapon; explain.

answer.exemplar: Attention narrows to the weapon, reducing encoding of the perpetrator's face and other details, impairing later identification.

questions.explanation: Weapon focus narrows attention to the threat, leaving fewer resources for encoding the perpetrator's features. This impairs identification.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the primacy effect in impression formation
questions.stem: Clinician notes a first impression dominates even after contradictory later information; what effect?
questions.explanation: Early information weighing more heavily than later information is the primacy effect in impression formation. It shapes lasting impressions.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician notes a patient follows orders by seeing themselves as an instrument of authority.

questions.stem: What concept explains this?
questions.explanation: Seeing oneself as an agent carrying out another's wishes is the agentic state. It helps explain obedience to harmful orders.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

stimulus.body: Clinician diagrams a patient performing a simple task better when observed.

questions.stem: What phenomenon is shown?

options.misconception: confuses performance gain with effort reduction

questions.explanation: Improved performance on simple tasks when observed is social facilitation, driven by arousal. Complex tasks may suffer instead.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Clinician wants to test whether people exert less effort in groups; design a study.

answer.exemplar: Compare individual effort on a task when working alone versus in a group, holding accountability constant, to measure social loafing.

questions.explanation: Comparing alone versus group effort isolates social loafing. Holding accountability constant rules out alternative explanations.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish social facilitation from social loafing
questions.stem: Clinician asks how social facilitation differs from social loafing; explain.

answer.exemplar: Social facilitation improves individual performance when observed, especially on simple tasks, whereas social loafing reduces effort when working in a group with pooled output.

questions.explanation: Facilitation concerns individual performance under observation; loafing concerns effort reduction in collective tasks. The contexts and outcomes differ.
questions.hint: Performance under observation versus effort in groups.
questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
